{{Short description|Theorem in harmonic analysis}}
In [[mathematics]], the '''Riemann–Lebesgue lemma''', named after [[Bernhard Riemann]] and [[Henri Lebesgue]], states that the [[Fourier transform]] or [[Laplace transform]] of an [[Lp space|''L''<sup>1</sup> function]] [[Vanish at infinity|vanishes at infinity]]. It is of importance in [[harmonic analysis]] and [[asymptotic analysis]].

== Statement ==
Let <math>f\in L^1(\R^n)</math> be an integrable function, i.e. <math>f\colon\R^n \rightarrow \C</math> is a [[measurable function]] such that
:<math>\|f\|_{L^1} = \int_{\R^n} |f(x)| \mathrm{d}x < \infty, </math>
and let <math>\hat{f}</math> be the Fourier transform of <math>f</math>, i.e.
:<math>\hat{f}\colon\R^n \rightarrow \C, \ \xi\mapsto \int_{\R^n} f(x) \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}x\cdot\xi}\mathrm{d}x.</math>
Then <math>\hat{f}</math> vanishes at infinity: <math>|\hat{f}(\xi)| \to 0</math> as <math> |\xi| \to\infty </math>.

Because the Fourier transform of an integrable function is continuous, the Fourier transform <math>\hat{f}</math> is a continuous function vanishing at infinity. If <math>C_0(\R^n)</math> denotes the vector space of continuous functions vanishing at infinity, the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma may be formulated as follows: The Fourier transformation maps <math>L^1(\R^n)</math> to <math>C_0(\R^n)</math>.

=== Proof ===
We will focus on the one-dimensional case <math>n=1</math>, the proof in higher dimensions is similar. First, suppose that <math>f</math> is continuous and [[compactly supported]]. For <math>\xi \neq 0</math>, the substitution <math>\textstyle x\to x+\frac{\pi}{\xi}</math> leads to
:<math>\hat{f}(\xi) = \int_{\R} f(x) \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}x\xi}\mathrm{d}x = \int_{\R} f\left(x+\frac{\pi}{\xi}\right) \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}x\xi} \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}\pi} \mathrm{d}x = -\int_{\R} f\left(x+\frac{\pi}{\xi}\right) \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}x\xi} \mathrm{d}x </math>.
This gives a second formula for <math>\hat{f}(\xi)</math>. Taking the mean of both formulas, we arrive at the following estimate:
:<math>|\hat{f}(\xi)|\le \frac{1}{2}\int_{\R} \left|f(x)-f\left(x+\frac{\pi}{\xi}\right)\right|\mathrm{d}x</math>.
When <math>f</math> is continuous, <math>\left|f(x)-f\left(x+\tfrac{\pi}{\xi}\right)\right|</math> converges to <math>0</math> as <math>|\xi| \to \infty</math> for all <math>x \in \R</math>. Thus, <math>|\hat{f}(\xi)|</math> converges to 0 as <math>|\xi| \to \infty</math> due to the [[dominated convergence theorem]].

Now, if <math>f</math> is an arbitrary integrable function, it may be approximated in the <math>L^1</math> norm by a compactly supported continuous function. For <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>, pick a compactly supported continuous function <math>g</math> such that <math>\|f-g\|_{L^1} \leq \varepsilon</math>. Then
:<math> \limsup_{\xi\rightarrow\pm\infty} |\hat{f}(\xi)| \leq  \limsup_{\xi\to\pm\infty}  \left|\int (f(x)-g(x))\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}x\xi} \, \mathrm{d}x\right| + \limsup_{\xi\rightarrow\pm\infty}  \left|\int g(x)\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{i}x\xi} \, \mathrm{d}x\right| \leq \varepsilon + 0 = \varepsilon.</math>
Since <math>g</math> is continuous, we have <math>\hat{g}\to 0</math>, because of RL lemma shown above for continuous functions. Because this holds for any <math>\varepsilon > 0</math>, it follows that <math>|\hat{f}(\xi)| \to 0</math> as <math> |\xi| \to\infty </math>.

==Other versions==
The Riemann–Lebesgue lemma holds in a variety of other situations.

* If <math>f \in L^1[0,\infty)</math>, then the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma also holds for the Laplace transform of <math>f</math>, that is,
::<math>\int_0^\infty f(t) \mathrm{e}^{-tz} \mathrm{d}t \to 0</math>
:as <math>|z| \to \infty</math> within the half-plane <math>\mathrm{Re}(z) \geq 0</math>.

* A version holds for [[Fourier series]] as well: if <math>f</math> is an integrable function on a bounded interval, then the [[Fourier coefficient|Fourier coefficients]] <math>\hat{f}_k </math> of <math>f</math> tend to 0 as <math>k \to \pm \infty </math>. This follows by extending <math>f</math> by zero outside the interval, and then applying the version of the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma on the entire real line.

* However, the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma does not hold for arbitrary distributions. For example, the Dirac delta function distribution formally has a finite integral over the real line, but its Fourier transform is a constant and does not vanish at infinity.

==Applications==
The Riemann–Lebesgue lemma can be used to prove the validity of asymptotic approximations for integrals. Rigorous treatments of the [[method of steepest descent]] and the [[method of stationary phase]], amongst others, are based on the Riemann–Lebesgue lemma.
